content: This group met both virtually and in person from October 25–27, 2022, in Geneva, Switzerland. The recommendations outlined in this guideline will be updated as new evidence becomes available. The initial focus of this publication is on healthcare facility settings, with future updates planned to address community settings and those used by special populations. Recommendations related to healthcare settings that include discussions on community settings have been incorporated into this document. While many recommendations have been updated in this version, some from the 2014 and 2016 IPC guidelines have also been included. If a previous recommendation has been carried forward, it has been clearly flagged. A summary of nine previous recommendations included in this guideline is provided in Table 1, while new recommendations are summarized in Table 2. Key Recommendations and Practices: 1. Hand Hygiene: WHO strongly recommends performing hand hygiene using either alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and running water, following the correct technique. Alcohol-based hand rubs should be available at all points of care, including entrances and isolation rooms. If alcohol-based hand rubs are unavailable, soap and water should be used. When hands are visibly soiled, soap and water must always be used. In settings where bleach or chlorine solutions are currently used for hand hygiene, WHO recommends transitioning to alcohol-based hand rubs or soap and water. However, bleach/chlorine solutions may be used temporarily in emergency situations until other options become available. 2. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Mucous membranes of the eyes, mouth, and nose should be fully covered by PPE. Either a face shield or goggles should be used. A fluid-resistant particulate respirator is recommended during procedures that generate aerosols of body fluids. Nitrile gloves are preferred over latex gloves. For clothing protection, disposable gowns and aprons or disposable coveralls and aprons made of fabric resistant to penetration by blood and body fluids should be used. 3. Screening and Isolation: Patients with suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg disease should be isolated, preferably in single rooms, and healthcare workers should wear appropriate PPE. 4. Interaction with Families and Visitors: Once patients with suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg disease are isolated, interaction with family and visitors should be facilitated to promote well-being while preventing direct physical contact and providing education. 5. Healthcare Worker Attire: Healthcare workers in areas with suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg patients should wear medical scrubs and closed-toe shoes during their shifts. 6. Waste Management: All waste generated from the care of patients with suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg disease, including waste from decontamination processes, should be treated as infectious waste. Surfaces in healthcare facilities should be disinfected using the wiping method rather than spraying. 7. Handling of Human Remains: Disinfection of the body prior to handling or placing it in a body bag is not required. 8. Healthcare workers exposed to Ebola or Marburg viruses should be excluded from work for 21 days. 9. Research and Evidence: The guideline development process highlighted the limited evidence base for IPC practices during Ebola and Marburg outbreaks, which is often of low or very low certainty. The data from this study informed the GDG's decision-making process. 10. Guideline Development: The recommendations were developed using the GRADE methodology, which assesses the certainty of evidence based on factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. The guideline also incorporates foundational good practice statements reflecting best practices in IPC. Background on Ebola and Marburg Viruses: Ebola and Marburg viruses are enveloped RNA viruses belonging to the Filoviridae family. There are six species of Ebola virus, four of which cause disease in humans: Zaire ebolavirus, Sudan ebolavirus, Bundibugyo ebolavirus, and Taï Forest ebolavirus. Reston ebolavirus has been found in animal handlers but is not associated with clinical disease in humans. Bombali ebolavirus is not known to be pathogenic in humans. Marburg virus has one species, with two distinct viruses: Marburg virus (MARV) and Ravn virus (RAVV). Both diseases have high case fatality rates, averaging 50% but ranging from 24% to 90%, which can be reduced with optimized supportive care. Future Directions: The guideline will be developed in three phases: Phase 3 will focus on special populations and settings, such as maternal, child, survivor, and surgical settings. The aim is to align guidance with scientific evidence while considering field experiences and ensuring the best possible protection against filovirus infections. Disposable items are preferred to minimize handling of contaminated PPE, and the hierarchy of IPC principles, including engineering, environmental, and administrative controls, should be adhered to. This guideline represents an opportunity to align advice with evidence-based standards and transmission-based precautions, addressing gaps in current practices and ensuring optimal care delivery.
